introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.summary: Tachyon is a polyglot, file-system-routed full-stack framework distributed through the standalone ty binary. Tac is the frontend layer and Yon is the backend/runtime layer.

sections.heading: Install
sections.body: Tachyon ships as the standalone `ty` binary — no package manager or runtime toolchain required. The installer also pulls the `chex` (schema validation) and `ttid` (identifier generation) binaries it drives at runtime. Scaffold an app and start the shape-aware dev server: Tachyon detects whether your app has a client/, a server/, or both, and serves the right thing on one port.
sections.code:
curl -fsSL https://tachyon.del.ma/install.sh | sh
ty init my-app --name "My App"
cd my-app
ty serve

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: Pages live in client/pages, components in client/components, and backend routes in server/routes. A companion file sits beside its tac.html template; shared browser assets and data live under client/shared.
sections.code:
client/
  pages/tac.html
  components/hero/tac.html
  components/hero/tac.swift
  shared/assets/  shared/data/
server/
  routes/posts/yon.js

routing.title: Routing
routing.summary: Both layers route from the file system: a directory is a path, and dynamic segments use _slug directories that become :slug parameters at runtime.

sections.heading: Frontend pages
sections.body: client/pages/tac.html serves /, client/pages/docs/tac.html serves /docs, and client/pages/docs/_topic/tac.html serves /docs/:topic — the page you are reading uses exactly that dynamic segment. An ancestor page containing a slot element becomes a reusable shell for its descendants.
sections.code:
client/pages/
  tac.html          -> /
  docs/tac.html     -> /docs (shell with <slot />)
  docs/_topic/
    tac.html        -> /docs/:topic

sections.heading: Backend routes
sections.body: A route file at server/routes/<path>/yon.<ext> exports a Handler class whose static methods are HTTP verbs. One route can be split across languages with sibling yon files declaring non-overlapping verbs — the Tachyon repo's full-stack fixture app splits its /language route across JavaScript (GET/HEAD), Rust (POST/DELETE) and C++ (PUT/PATCH).

sections.heading: Handler protocol
sections.body: JavaScript and Python get class-style Handler adapters. Any other executable language can read one bounded JSON request from stdin and write one JSON response to stdout, with interpreters registered in .tachyonrc.

yon.title: Yon backend
yon.summary: Yon is Tachyon's backend/runtime layer: filesystem-routed handlers, one supervised process protocol, middleware, scheduled workers and durable SSE topic logs.

sections.heading: Serve modes
sections.body: ty serve is shape-aware. A client/ app serves frontend assets, a server/ app serves backend routes, and a client/ + server/ app runs full-stack.
sections.code:
ty serve
YON_PORT=8000 ty serve
YON_HOST=0.0.0.0 ty serve
NODE_ENV=production ty serve

sections.heading: Route convention
sections.body: Backend routes live at server/routes/<path>/yon.<ext>. A Handler class exposes static methods named after HTTP verbs. Dynamic path segments use _name folders and arrive in request.paths.

sections.heading: Languages
sections.body: JavaScript and Python get class-style Handler adapters. Ruby, Swift, Zig, shell scripts, prebuilt binaries and other languages run through the same JSON stdin/stdout protocol; .tachyonrc registers commands for non-executable sources.
sections.code:
.tachyonrc

[interpreters]
rb = ["ruby"]

sections.heading: Process lifecycle
sections.body: Yon invokes one bounded process per request. The supervisor enforces deadlines and body limits, captures bounded diagnostics, and terminates a child that outlives its request.
sections.code:
YON_HANDLER_TIMEOUT_MS=30000
YON_MAX_BODY_BYTES=1048576

sections.heading: Protocol response
sections.body: A handler returns a status, headers and body through Handler Protocol v1. Static fields and GET response values can also compose the bounded context for a colocated yon.html view.

sections.heading: Specification boundary
sections.body: The Rust rewrite does not generate OpenAPI or host /api-docs. Generate a specification in your application pipeline or keep the legacy server for those endpoints; ty migrate check reports this difference.
sections.code: ty migrate check .

sections.heading: Realtime topics
sections.body: A topic is a bounded append-only NDJSON log under .tachyon/topics. Browsers subscribe with EventSource, receive the log position as the event id and reconnect from the last position automatically.
sections.code:
const releases = new EventSource('/.tachyon/topics/releases')
releases.onmessage = (event) => console.log(event.lastEventId, event.data)

sections.heading: Security and middleware
sections.body: The server binds loopback by default, rejects traversal, applies security headers and bounds requests and child processes. Root middleware can answer before a route or merge and replace responses afterward.
sections.code:
ty serve
YON_HANDLER_TIMEOUT_MS=30000
YON_MAX_BODY_BYTES=1048576

sections.heading: Polyglot middleware
sections.body: Middleware uses the same process protocol as routes and may be written in any configured executable language. A 204 continues; another status answers early in before or replaces the response in after.
sections.code:
middleware/
  yon.rb
server/
  routes/
    items/yon.js

sections.heading: Middleware phases
sections.body: The before phase receives request metadata and can continue or answer early. The after phase also receives response metadata and can merge headers or replace the response. A failed after hook preserves the original response.
sections.code:
{ "phase": "before", "request": {}, "context": {} }
{ "phase": "after", "request": {}, "response": {}, "context": {} }

sections.heading: Raw shim middleware
sections.body: Any other language can skip the class adapter and use the raw protocol. The middleware file reads a JSON envelope from stdin and writes one JSON result to stdout. This is useful for Go, Swift, Zig, shell scripts, or a prebuilt binary.

sections.heading: Middleware envelopes
sections.body: Process middleware receives metadata-only envelopes so it cannot accidentally consume request bodies or break streaming responses. A 204 result continues or merges headers; any other status becomes the response.

sections.heading: Telemetry boundary
sections.body: The Rust rewrite does not emit OpenTelemetry spans. Instrument at your deployment boundary or keep the legacy server when emitted spans are a migration requirement; ty migrate check reports the difference.
sections.code: ty migrate check .

templates.title: Tac templates
templates.summary: Templates are HTML with braces for interpolation, on:event attributes for delegated events, loop, logic, and switch elements for control flow, and explicit island hydration policies.

sections.heading: Interpolation and events
sections.body: Braces use a bounded expression grammar with contextual escaping; authored source is never evaluated as JavaScript. Route-known values render on the server, while hydrated islands may defer text fields and method calls to their companion. Event bindings compile to structured data for one delegated listener per event type.
sections.code: {headline}

sections.heading: Control flow
sections.body: Loops, conditionals and switches are elements, so structure stays visible in the markup.
sections.code:
{post.title}

Ready.

Working…

Done.

sections.heading: Components
sections.body: A component folder under client/components maps to a hyphenated tag: components/panel/users becomes panel-users. Props pass as attributes, and hydrate="visible" activates an island when it approaches the viewport.

sections.heading: Island hydration
sections.body: A component occurrence with a literal hydrate policy is fully rendered on the server, then adopts that useful DOM in place when its browser companion activates. Use load for immediate activation, idle for background work, visible for viewport-driven activation, interaction for the first user intent, or never for permanently static server HTML. Repeated islands, including components inside loop, receive independent identities.
sections.code:
<product-card :product="product" hydrate="visible" />
<cart-summary hydrate="interaction" />
<legal-notice hydrate="never" />

sections.heading: Island contracts
sections.body: hydrate must be one of load, idle, visible, interaction, or never as a static literal. It cannot be dynamic or combined with lazy. Props must be JSON-serializable public data; never put secrets or authorization state in serialized island props. A failed activation leaves the server-rendered DOM in place and can retry on a later interaction.

native-rendering.title: Native HTML rendering
native-rendering.summary: Non-web Tac bundles keep HTML as the only application-facing view language, render supported semantics with native controls, and isolate only unmapped subtrees in local WebViews.

sections.heading: Native by default
sections.body: web remains a browser target. macos, windows, linux, ios, and android are always native-first. The compiler emits tachyon.native-ui.json for the initial versioned UI tree and tachyon.native-controller.js for live rendering and events; neither controller nor native nodes depend on a DOM.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos
ty bundle --target android
ty bundle --target windows

sections.heading: One HTML source
sections.body: Application developers still write tac.html. Before native tree creation, Tac lowers loop, logic, switch and case control elements, resolves Tac components, evaluates bindings, and removes nonvisual script, style, template, and noscript elements. Native hosts map the resulting semantic tree to SwiftUI on Apple platforms, Jetpack Compose on Android, WinUI on Windows, and GTK on Linux.
sections.code:
{title}

Selected: {selected}

sections.heading: Native-first tag handling
sections.body: Control tags and Tac component tags compile away before native output. Supported semantic HTML maps to native controls. Known standard HTML without a native mapping and unmapped Web Components automatically become isolated WebView boundaries; a genuinely unknown non-HTML tag still fails so typos remain visible. A semantic nativeUIAdapters mapping always wins over fallback.

sections.heading: Live events
sections.body: Each native host sends normalized input and event data to the generated controller, including elementId, type, value, checked, and detail. The controller applies the event, rerenders, and returns the complete next tree for the host to reconcile. JavaScriptCore runs the controller on macOS and iOS; Android, Windows, and Linux use embedded QuickJS runtimes.

sections.heading: Automatic local boundary
sections.body: The compiler keeps supported parents and siblings native while loading the nearest unmapped subtree in an isolated local WebView with bundled CSS and module entrypoints. No app-wide mode or fallback declaration is required. Truly unknown non-HTML tags still fail, and local boundaries do not grant raw nativeCapabilities, devicePermissions, managed content origins, or native host extensions.

sections.heading: Managed remote content
sections.body: Desktop bundles can open authenticated HTTPS sites through contentSurface when their exact origins are declared. The active managed surface is composed into the right 75% of the primary native window, beside trusted Tac controls, so appWindow always-on-top and opacity apply to the complete presentation; click-through and capture protection do too on macOS and Windows. Additional open surfaces remain isolated and the most recently opened surface occupies the composed pane. Each surface uses an isolated WebKit/WebView2/WebKitGTK context, enforces the origin allowlist on every navigation, denies popups, and never receives the application's native bridge. Camera and microphone requests are allowed only when both the device permission and requesting origin are declared.

companions.title: Companions
companions.summary: A tac.js or tac.ts file beside a hydrated component becomes its browser-side island instance; bounded fields and methods remain explicit.

sections.heading: Island fields
sections.body: The server renders everything it can from route context and props. Inside a hydrated island, unresolved text expressions are encoded as bounded expression trees and refreshed after event handlers run. Structure and dynamic attributes still need server-known values or an explicit hydrate hook.

sections.heading: Browser lifecycle and storage
sections.body: hydrate(root, signal) is the explicit browser lifecycle. Use standards such as sessionStorage, localStorage and CustomEvent directly; the AbortSignal gives listeners and asynchronous work a deterministic teardown boundary.

polyglot.title: Polyglot companions
polyglot.summary: Component companions can be compiled by real native-language toolchains and exposed to browser islands through one bounded ABI.

sections.heading: Choose a companion language
sections.body: A browser component may use tac.js, tac.ts, tac.dart, tac.rs, tac.kt, tac.swift, or tac.cs beside tac.html. JavaScript and TypeScript emit modules; Rust, Dart, Kotlin, Swift and C# are compiled by rustc, dart, kotlinc-js, swiftc and dotnet rather than by a Tachyon language subset.
sections.code:
client/components/counter/
  tac.html
  tac.swift

var count = 6
func doubled() -> Int { count * 2 }
let tac: [String: TacMember] = [
  "count": .field({ count }, { count = $0 as? Int ?? count }),
  "doubled": .method({ _ in doubled() }),
]

sections.heading: Declare the ABI
sections.body: A native-language companion declares the readable fields, writable fields and callable methods its island may reach. The host exposes those members through get, set and call operations, so it never guesses from reflection and never evaluates companion source.

sections.heading: Contracts stay on the server
sections.body: OPTIONS.schema.json remains the Yon route contract for incoming requests and outgoing responses. Browser companions are UI controllers, so JavaScript and TypeScript use normal browser HTTP APIs rather than declaring a second route protocol.

sections.heading: Toolchain boundary
sections.body: The WebAssembly ABI intentionally exposes data and methods, not an implicit browser or native SDK. Keep browser APIs in JavaScript or TypeScript islands and keep native host capabilities behind the generated platform controller. A missing toolchain fails the build with ty doctor guidance.
sections.code:
ty doctor
ty build

# Native-language browser companions require matching compilers:
# rustc, dart, kotlinc-js, swiftc + WebAssembly SDK, or dotnet

devices.title: Devices and targets
devices.summary: Tac builds one client source tree into a browser output or native desktop and mobile controls. The rooted terminology: platform is the form factor (desktop/mobile/web); environment and os are synonyms for the concrete host (windows/macos/linux/android/ios/web); target is the bundle output.

sections.heading: Targets
sections.body: The supported bundle targets are web, macos, windows, linux, ios and android. web emits browser assets; every non-web target uses the native renderer by default. The all target expands to every supported target and writes sibling directories under dist/.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target web      # dist/web
ty bundle --target macos    # dist/macos
ty bundle --target windows  # dist/windows
ty bundle --target linux    # dist/linux
ty bundle --target ios      # dist/ios
ty bundle --target android  # dist/android
ty bundle --target all

sections.heading: One native-first policy
sections.body: Every non-web target maps supported Tac HTML to platform controls and automatically isolates the nearest unmapped standard HTML or Web Component subtree in a local WebView. Native siblings remain native. The former render-mode flag and TAC_RENDER_MODE override have been removed.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos    # SwiftUI + inferred local boundaries
ty bundle --target android  # Compose + inferred local boundaries
ty bundle --target windows  # WinUI + inferred local boundaries

sections.heading: Preview
sections.body: Preview accepts exactly one target. If you omit --target, Tachyon previews web. Native previews run prerequisite checks first so missing Xcode or Swift, the Android SDK, Windows build tools, GTK, embedded controller dependencies, or a WebView dependency required by an inferred boundary fail early with an actionable message.
sections.code:
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos
ty preview --target android

sections.heading: Runtime globals
sections.body: Templates can read platform, environment, os and target without imports. Every companion language can read the same structured context through its Tac runtime binding.
sections.code:
<switch :value="platform">
  <case :when="'desktop'">Desktop bundle on {os}</case>
  <case :when="'mobile'">Mobile bundle on {os}</case>
  <case default>Web platform</case>
</switch>

const platform = this.tac.platform.platform  // desktop | mobile | web
const os = this.tac.platform.os              // windows | macos | linux | android | ios | web

sections.heading: Rooted terminology
sections.body: platform is the form factor: macos, windows and linux targets are the desktop platform; ios and android are the mobile platform; web is the web platform. environment and os are synonyms for the concrete host: the operating system for native bundles, web for browser bundles (the detected visitor OS stays on browserOS). target names the bundle output. Companion language names the language a Tac companion is written in: JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Kotlin, Swift or C#.

storage.title: Storage and data
storage.summary: Tac caches reads in the browser and Yon streams live updates over Server-Sent Events.

sections.heading: Live subscriptions
sections.body: subscribe() runs an initial find, listens to the browser-local mirror for same-tab mutations, and follows the server event stream for remote changes — falling back to polling when SSE is unavailable.

sections.heading: Realtime mailboxes
sections.body: Yon realtime persists messages into durable append-only queues and delivers them over Server-Sent Events; reconnecting clients replay from their last cursor, so offline browsers never lose messages.

cookbook.title: Cookbook
cookbook.summary: Concrete recipes for building Tachyon apps without leaving the frontend-first workflow. This website is frontend-only, so these patterns can be explored with Tac companions before a Yon server exists.

sections.heading: Frontend-only prototype
sections.body: Start with client/ only. Tac renders pages and components, and companions provide the reactive UI controller. When you later add server/routes, the UI contract can stay the same.
sections.code:
client/
  pages/tac.html
  components/panel/users/tac.html
  components/panel/users/tac.kt
  shared/data/docs.json
db/
  schemas/users/manifest.json

sections.heading: Event-driven islands
sections.body: Browser CustomEvent provides explicit communication between islands. A form can dispatch a collection change and interested islands can subscribe through their hydrate AbortSignal without knowing who sent it.

sections.heading: Polyglot middleware boundary
sections.body: When the frontend prototype grows a Yon server, add middleware at server/middleware/yon.<ext>. Class-style middleware works for the supported adapter languages, and the raw JSON shim lets a team keep an existing policy engine in another executable language.

sections.heading: Native target polish
sections.body: Author semantic HTML once, then bundle web, desktop and mobile outputs. The native planner lowers supported structure into platform controls and isolates only unmapped subtrees in local WebView boundaries.
sections.code:
Workspace

ty bundle --target macos ty bundle --target android

operations.title: Operations
operations.summary: Loopback-safe serving, bounded child processes, middleware phases, deterministic builds and stable diagnostics form the operational baseline.

sections.heading: Diagnostics and migration evidence
sections.body: Compiler, server and toolchain failures use stable TY diagnostics with bounded details. ty doctor reports companion toolchains and ty migrate check records intentional compatibility changes before cutover.

sections.heading: Build and deploy
sections.body: ty bundle writes dist/web by default. Use --target all during release validation, then preview or package the individual target you intend to ship.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target all
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos

sections.heading: Security
sections.body: Security headers, loopback-only default binding, traversal rejection, request limits and handler deadlines are enforced by the Rust server. Application authentication and API schema generation stay explicit deployment concerns.

platform-apis.title: Platform APIs
platform-apis.summary: The web target uses standards-backed helpers, while desktop native-first bundles expose audited platform adapters through the same public Tac facades.

sections.heading: Current target availability
sections.body: Browser output can use storage, fetch, clipboard, file selection, geolocation, notifications, and media when the browser supports them. capabilities.supports reports whether an operation is available, and capabilities.state reports granted, denied, prompt, or unsupported where a permission state exists.

sections.heading: Desktop native capability matrix
sections.body: macOS, Windows, and Linux implement app information, clipboard, external HTTP(S) URLs, always-on-top state, opacity, global shortcuts, click-through, and declared screen capture. Linux selects its backend at runtime: Wayland uses the XDG GlobalShortcuts and Screenshot portals with explicit user consent, while X11 uses an audited XGrabKey shortcut fallback; GTK applies an empty native input region for click-through. capabilities.state reports prompt or unsupported when a required portal or compositor feature is absent. Capture protection remains macOS/Windows-only because Linux has no enforceable cross-compositor contract. All three desktop hosts compose allowlisted managed content into the primary window's declared 25/75 split, and remote surfaces never receive the bridge. macOS alone currently implements explicitly requested raw filesystem and shell operations. iOS and Android remain fail-closed for privileged native-tree declarations.

sections.heading: Generated manifest is authoritative
sections.body: tachyon.host.json lists only concrete operations for the selected target. The DOM-free native controller receives the same list from its host bridge, so capabilities.supports and capabilities.state cannot claim an adapter that the packaged host omitted. Unsupported device permissions, raw nativeCapabilities, and permission origins outside managedContentOrigins stop the build.

sections.heading: Companion boundary
sections.body: JavaScript and TypeScript browser islands can use standards-backed browser APIs directly. Native-language WebAssembly companions expose only the fields and methods they declare in their tac member map; native host capabilities remain in the generated platform controller rather than an implicit language prelude.

sections.heading: Events and isolated WebViews
sections.body: host.on is the typed event channel for native events such as shortcut.activated. In a DOM-free native controller, companion @onMount methods run after the host bridge is ready, so they can subscribe with host.on, register shortcuts, and call contentSurface.open during startup without constructor delays. Automatic local fallback boundaries and managed remote-content surfaces are deliberately isolated: neither receives the application-wide native bridge. Linux requires xdg-desktop-portal plus a desktop-specific backend for Wayland shortcuts and capture; Debian/Ubuntu builds also require libgtk-3-dev, libjson-glib-dev, and libx11-dev. Validate both Wayland and Xorg sessions by checking capability state, registering and firing a recovery shortcut, toggling click-through, and completing a window-picker capture. Native host extensions, mobile privileged adapters, and biometrics remain unavailable until each target has an audited implementation.
